extracted.intended_audience: students, contributors, and readers of 19th-century mathematical journals (geometry/analysis practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and methodological guidance for solving and proving classical geometry and conic-section problems (journal exercise solutions). Emphasises multiple solution methods, analytic identities, and cautions about proof techniques using arbitrary coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of independent methods for demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: The young geometer will do well to exercise himself in the demonstration of this theorem by any independent method that may occur to him; perhaps the transversal method will furnish the simplest method that can be devised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages finding independent/alternative proofs rather than relying on a single approach. Suggests the transversal method as a likely simple approach for the stated theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit 3D (spatial) viewpoints to simplify plane problems
rubrics_metrics.description: From the contemplation of the properties of figures situate in space we may often deduce with great simplicity, properties of plane figures which it would require considerable labour to demonstrate in reference to them initially viewed as plane figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a plane-figure theorem is awkward to prove directly, consider embedding the figure in space or using descriptive-geometry viewpoints; spatial constructions can make certain plane relations immediate (example: Monge, Chasles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate geometric conditions into analytic 'conditions of identity'
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions of identity (a) form the readiest and most convenient means of proving any properties that may be predicated of this curious figure. They are the analytical expressions of the condition that the three diagonals of the hexagon intersect in the same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert geometric concurrency/incidence conditions into algebraic identities (equations) and use them as primary tools; algebraic identity manipulations can be the most convenient path to the desired geometric property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch the figure to reveal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: By sketching the figure it will be seen that Ui = 0, M2 = 0, Uz = 0, are the equations to the first, third, and fifth sides ; and Vi = 0, «?2 = 0, v^ = 0, those of the sides respectively opposite to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings/diagrams often immediately reveal which equations/relations correspond to elements of the figure; use sketches early to guide algebraic set-up and to check which lines/points correspond to which analytic equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution using the method of arbitrary coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: If in any inquiry having reference to surfaces that have eight points common, we can shew by the method of arbitrary coefficients, that a property holds in each case, that is, when each coefficient is arbitrary, all we prove is that it is true for some particular positions of the eight points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitrary-coefficients arguments can hide special positioning: demonstrating a property with some coefficients left 'arbitrary' may still only establish the result for particular configurations. One must check whether the arbitrariness actually yields generality or merely special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer arbitrary multipliers for genuine generality
rubrics_metrics.description: It is indeed very probable, that a property thus investigated, is generally true; but a safer mode of demonstration in such cases is by an arbitrary multiplier (see p. 12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When trying to prove a general theorem about families of curves/surfaces, use the arbitrary-multiplier approach rather than treating coefficients as arbitrary parameters; this gives a safer path to general proofs and avoids the special-position pitfalls of arbitrary-coefficient methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: To disprove general properties, exhibit particular counterexamples via arbitrary coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: We prove, very readily, the failure of the property in some particular cases, and hence its failure in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The arbitrary-coefficients method can be effective for finding particular cases where a purported general property fails; a single genuine counterexample obtained this way shows the general property is false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate factors to zero unless indeterminacy conditions hold
rubrics_metrics.description: We would be justified in equating to zero each factor of that result as I have done. This we could do only when each factor is indeterminate in the ordinary sense, that is, when each factor involves variables that are functions of each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unjustified step of setting algebraic factors individually to zero when deriving geometric conclusions unless one can justify that those factors are indeterminate (involve dependent variables). Otherwise such factorization leads to invalid inferences about general cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple valid solution methods and cross-check
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple distinct solutions are given for the same problem (e.g., moments of inertia: using principal axes, projection to an ellipse, direct integration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide or seek multiple independent methods (symmetry/principal axes, geometric projection, integration, analytic identities) to solve or verify a result; different approaches serve as cross-checks and may illuminate different aspects of the problem.
